name: Wendy Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good morning, Wendy. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you tell me is confidential. Is now a good time?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, it's fine. Lukas is in the workshop, so the house is quiet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's Lukas, and what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Lukas is my fiancé; he's a carpenter and has his own workshop behind the house. I translate French into English, mostly for three wine exporters in our valley: labels, export forms, tasting notes, the letters to importers abroad. I also translate the newsletter and appeal letters for our parish charity, partly paid and partly volunteer. I work at the old oak desk in the front room, with a notebook and my grandmother's French dictionary.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the tasting notes, finding the right English for a wine that smells of 'sous-bois', the floor of a forest after rain. I grew up among vines, my parents have a few hectares, so I know what the winemakers mean. What wears me out is the export forms, all codes and numbers. I'm still slow, and the exporters sometimes send things back because I've used a word an English buyer wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That sounds like how it should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people still want a person who knows the wine and the families. I'd say it after Mass to anyone who asks, and at the exporters' Christmas dinner. I don't go online much, so that's where I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad and not much more. The exporters here have known my family for years, and they'd rather send work to the Bauer girl than to a machine. Lukas's workshop is busy, we have savings, and my parents' land is behind us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, and I'd try to get better at the export forms, maybe by asking old Mr Girard at the first exporter to sit with me for an afternoon. I'd keep the charity work as it is. And we'd carry on saving for the wedding next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really. This is the life I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the family connection matter to your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More than my skill, if I'm honest, because I'm still learning. The exporters in our valley would rather send work to the Bauer girl than to a machine. I know I have to earn that trust over time, but it's a good start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any pressure at all in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the wedding costs, and they're manageable. We've saved for two years. My mother keeps adding cousins to the list, but that's family, not money trouble.

steps.text: Keep translating for the three valley wine exporters
Ask an older exporter to coach her on export forms
Keep saving for the wedding next summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds more worrying. Let me think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses should do what's sensible, but they shouldn't forget people who've worked for them faithfully. I wouldn't ask the government to fix it. I'd say families and communities have to look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, export forms and letters are exactly what that card describes, and I'm junior and slow at them. The younger son at one exporter already talks about using AI for everything. I think I'd lose the forms within a couple of years, maybe a third of my income, and keep the tasting notes only while the old men run the firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with the clients I have and not chase anything new yet. I'd offer to do the paperwork and invoices for Lukas's workshop, so he stops doing them at midnight. And I'd wait and see before spending money on any course, because I don't trust that whatever I learn won't change again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd pray about it, honestly. And I'd lean on Lukas more than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never use AI tools. Would that hold here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'm not good with new technology, and I don't want to be. If the work goes, I'd rather do something honest with my hands or for the family than spend my days checking a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lukas that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lukas, my fiancé, that I might earn less, and that I'm sorry. Lukas would say his grandfather built that workshop with nothing, and we'll manage. He'd mean it, and I'd still feel bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Before we've even been married two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's in God's hands, but people still have to work hard and look after their own. I'd say communities need to stick together. I wouldn't be asking for handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, all my translation is thinking work, so it's gone by 2028. The exporters would use a machine for the labels and notes, even the old ones, once it's as good and cheaper. Lukas's carpentry has about three years more, until the robots, and after that I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my parents if I can work properly on the vineyard, pruning and the harvest and the cellar, because that's hands-on. We'd make the wedding smaller and keep the money. And we'd talk about having children sooner, while Lukas still has the workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake next to Lukas, doing sums. But I'd also feel there are people around us who'd catch us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A smaller wedding. What would that mean, concretely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eighty guests instead of a hundred and forty, and the dinner in my parents' barn instead of the hotel. That saves maybe twelve thousand. My mother would be upset about the cousins, but she'd understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask your parents for vineyard work. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father would say yes before I finished asking. Pruning vines in February with my dad is cold, hard work, but nobody has ever needed a translator to do it. That's a comfort, in a strange way.

say: It's in **God's hands**, but people must still work hard.
Communities need to **stick together**; I wouldn't ask for handouts.
think: All my translation is **thinking work**, gone by 2028.
Lukas's **carpentry** has about three more years, until the robots.

Cut the wedding to **eighty guests** in her parents' barn.
feel: Also held by **family** who'd catch them.

fieldNote: She expects to **lose all translation** and falls back on the family land.

Her **wedding and children** plans shift with the timeline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a little better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a time for families to plan carefully and work hard, not to panic. I'd say it to my parish friends and at the exporters' dinners. I'd tell younger people to learn a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years means I translate until about 2030, while the exporters still trust me, and then it's over. I'd have time to learn the vineyard properly. And Lukas has until about 2034 before robots touch carpentry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep translating and save as much of it as I can, maybe 600 a month into the account for the house. I'd start helping in the cellar at harvest each autumn, to learn from my father. And we'd keep the wedding as planned, but buy a smaller house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, in a steadier way. I could see the shape of the next years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a smaller house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't want a mortgage that needs two incomes when one of the incomes is ending in 2031. Lukas wanted the house with the big garage. We'd find a compromise, probably a small house with a big shed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your mind about AI tools with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know that sounds stubborn. I'd rather use five years to learn the vines than learn a tool that's going to take my job anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's nearly a normal life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do things properly: work, raise a family, learn a trade, look after each other. I'd say it calmly. I'd be glad it wasn't the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have about eight good years of translating, and by then I'd hope to have children and be doing less anyway. Lukas would have workshop work until about 2039. That's most of the years we'd have small children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with the exporters and get properly good at the export forms. We'd marry as planned and try for children within two or three years. And I'd wait and see how it goes before I change anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only a little. More like something on a far horizon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about work, one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children to learn something with their hands, like their father, as well as their books. And to stay close to family, because that's what catches you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Mr Girard's son, who's going to run the first exporter. He's very keen on AI. I'd worry he'd sell the firm to someone big and the valley would lose another family business.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would hit just as Lukas and I are starting our married life. What would help is local firms staying in local hands, and apprenticeships for adults in real trades, like winemaking and carpentry, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the charity letters. When our parish writes to families who've lost someone, the words matter. I wouldn't want a machine writing those, even if it wrote them well.

headlineQuote: When our parish writes to families who've lost someone, the words matter.
portrait: Wendy is a 27-year-old **French-English** translator for wine exporters and her parish charity.
She's engaged to **Lukas**, a carpenter, and grew up on her parents' vineyard.
She never uses **AI tools** and relies on family trust more than skill.
In fast scenarios she'd turn to **vineyard work** and reshape wedding and children plans.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, hitting just as she and Lukas start married life.
whatWouldHelp: **Adult apprenticeships** in real trades, not handouts.
